                    ### Question
                    A 44-year-old woman presents with palpitations and lightheadedness. She says that symptoms onset 3 days ago and have not improved. She denies any similar episodes in this past. Her blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, heart rate is 150/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, and temperature is 36.6℃ (97.9℉). An ECG is performed and the results are shown in the picture. For cardioversion, it is decided to use an antiarrhythmic agent which has a use-dependent effect. Which of the following medications was most probably used?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Flecainide
opb. Amiodarone
opc. Diltiazem
opd. Propranolol
ope. Verapamil

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with tachycardia (heart rate of 150/min) and lightheadedness, indicating a possible arrhythmia, likely atrial fibrillation or flutter. Antiarrhythmic therapy is indicated for cardioversion. Use-dependence refers to the increased effectiveness of certain antiarrhythmic agents at higher heart rates. Flecainide is a well-known use-dependent antiarrhythmic agent, making it a likely choice for this patient. Amiodarone, while effective, does not primarily exhibit use-dependence. Diltiazem and Verapamil are calcium channel blockers and do not have a use-dependent effect. Propranolol is a beta-blocker and also does not exhibit use-dependence. Therefore, the most probable medication used for cardioversion in this case is Flecainide, supported by its known use-dependence in treating tachyarrhythmias.
